raw_text:
Heart failure (HF) remains a major global public health challenge, causing high morbidity and mortality. Its pathophysiology involves chronic neurohormonal dysregulation, notably of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS), the sympathetic nervous system, and the natriuretic peptide system [1]. Angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibition (ARNI) represents a landmark pharmacological advancement in heart failure management. Sacubitril/valsartan, the first-in-class ARNI, combines the neprilysin inhibitor prodrug sacubitril with the angiotensin II type 1 (AT1) receptor blocker valsartan [1]. Neprilysin is a membrane-bound endopeptidase that degrades various endogenous vasoactive peptides, including atrial, brain, and C-type natriuretic peptides, bradykinin, substance P, and adrenomedullin [2]. Because neprilysin also degrades angiotensin II, its inhibition must be combined with valsartan to prevent counterregulatory vasoconstriction [1,2]. Concomitant ACE and neprilysin inhibition is contraindicated due to high angioedema risk, requiring a 36-hour washout period when switching to sacubitril/valsartan [3].

In patients with chronic heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF), the landmark PARADIGM-HF trial established the superiority of sacubitril/valsartan over enalapril [1]. Patients randomized to sacubitril/valsartan experienced a 20% relative risk reduction in the primary composite endpoint of cardiovascular (CV) death or first HF hospitalization [1]. This clinical benefit was driven by robust reductions in both sudden cardiac death and death from worsening HF [4]. Furthermore, sacubitril/valsartan slowed clinical progression [5] and preserved renal function, slowing the decline in estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) compared to enalapril [6]. In the PROVE-HF trial, sacubitril/valsartan promoted left ventricular reverse remodeling, which strongly correlated with rapid N-terminal pro-brain natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP) reductions [7]. The EVALUATE-HF trial showed that while sacubitril/valsartan did not significantly reduce central aortic stiffness at 12 weeks compared to enalapril, it improved diastolic parameters [8]. It also significantly enhances quality of life, as evidenced by Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire scores [9]. However, in patients with chronic advanced HFrEF (NYHA class IV), the LIFE trial demonstrated that sacubitril/valsartan was not superior to valsartan alone in reducing NT-proBNP or improving clinical composite outcomes, indicating potential limits to its efficacy in end-stage cardiorenal disease [10].

For patients hospitalized with acute decompensated heart failure (ADHF), the PIONEER-HF trial demonstrated that in-hospital initiation after hemodynamic stabilization significantly reduced NT-proBNP concentrations compared to enalapril [11] and decreased post-discharge clinical events [12]. The TRANSITION trial showed that initiating sacubitril/valsartan either in-hospital or shortly after discharge was equally feasible, safe, and associated with high rates of target dose attainment [13]. The TITRATION study confirmed that both rapid (3-week) and gradual (6-week) up-titration regimens are well-tolerated in HFrEF [14].

The clinical utility of sacubitril/valsartan has also been evaluated across the spectrum of left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF). In the PARAGON-HF trial (LVEF ≥45%), sacubitril/valsartan narrowly missed statistical significance for the primary endpoint of total HF hospitalizations and CV death [15]. However, subgroup analyses suggested therapeutic benefit in women and patients with below-normal ejection fraction (LVEF ≤57%) [15]. A pooled analysis of PARADIGM-HF and PARAGON-HF confirmed a continuous therapeutic benefit extending into the mildly reduced ejection fraction (HFmrEF) range up to an LVEF of approximately 57–60% [16]. Although the PARALLAX trial demonstrated that sacubitril/valsartan significantly reduced NT-proBNP compared to individualized medical therapy in patients with LVEF ≥40%, it did not improve 6-minute walk distance [17]. Meta-analyses have consolidated these findings, validating the efficacy and safety of ARNI in both HFmrEF and lower-spectrum HFpEF [18]. Conversely, post-myocardial infarction, the PARADISE-MI trial showed that sacubitril/valsartan did not significantly reduce CV death or incident HF compared to ramipril [19].

Real-world registry data have mirrored these clinical trial findings. The European ARIADNE registry confirmed that outpatient sacubitril/valsartan use is associated with improved symptoms and significant LVEF improvement in routine practice [20]. Swedish Heart Failure Registry (SwedeHF) analyses showed that over 75% of HFrEF outpatients are eligible for ARNI [21], and expanding use across the ejection fraction spectrum captures a substantial portion of the broader HF population [22]. In Asian cohorts, the TAROT-HF registry verified the effectiveness of sacubitril/valsartan [23] and its role in promoting reverse remodeling and potentially reducing the clinical necessity of cardiac resynchronization therapy [24]. Nonetheless, implementation gaps remain; real-world medication adherence is tightly coupled with post-discharge outcomes [25]. While concerns over angioedema persist, real-world data demonstrate that the risk with sacubitril/valsartan is low and comparable to standard RAAS inhibitors [26]. From an economic perspective, ARNI therapy is highly cost-effective, offering substantial quality-adjusted life year (QALY) gains [27]. Cross-trial analyses estimate that comprehensive ARNI-based therapy adds 2.7 to 8.3 years of overall survival depending on age [28].

Consequently, contemporary guidelines have positioned sacubitril/valsartan as a foundational first-line therapy. The 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA guidelines recommend ARNI as a Class 1 therapy for symptomatic chronic HFrEF, preferring it over ACE inhibitors or ARBs, with Class 2b recommendations for HFmrEF and HFpEF with below-normal LVEF [29]. Similarly, the 2021 ESC guidelines establish sacubitril/valsartan as a cornerstone of HFrEF management to reduce hospitalizations and mortality [30].
